bibliography.abstract: Accurately estimating de facto population in dynamic urban environments is essential for predictive planning, service provision, and Smart City resilience, particularly in areas with strong seasonal fluctuations. Census-based approaches lack temporal resolution and overlook transient populations, while alternative methods often rely on restricted data, high computational demands, or indirect proxies. This study presents a scalable computational framework for estimating de facto urban population at monthly resolution by integrating high-resolution smart-meter water consumption records with census data, climatic normalization, and tourism indicators. The approach integrates IoT-based remote-reading records, supply-contract databases, census information, and official accommodation registers within an end-to-end ETL pipeline to infer monthly population variations in Alicante (Spain) between 2022 and 2024. A thermal-correction model isolates temperature-driven changes in water demand, improving estimation accuracy. K-means clustering with Dynamic Time Warping identifies neighborhood-level seasonal patterns, distinguishing stable residential areas, high-tourism zones, and districts with marked summer vacancy. Results reveal a robust methodology for population estimation, rigorously verified through out-of-sample validation for 2024, yielding a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 6.34% and an R 2 = 0.9874. Between January and July 2024, Alicante experienced an estimated 8.78% population increase (+32,749 people). Coastal tourist neighborhoods showed summer rises above 50%, whereas central medium-to-high-income areas exhibited declines up to −22.2% due to seasonal displacement to second residences. Consolidated residential areas remained stable year-round, with deviations below 5%. The methodology offers a low-cost, high-resolution, and privacy-preserving tool for strategic decision-making in Smart Cities and is fully replicable in urban contexts equipped with domestic smart-metering infrastructure to capture resident and floating population dynamics.
bibliography.title: Data-driven urban planning: Real population estimation using water consumption records and tourism data

en.caveats: The methodology is dependent on the presence of domestic smart-metering infrastructure, limiting its immediate application to cities already equipped with this technology.
en.what: The study developed a computational framework to estimate monthly de facto urban populations by combining smart-meter water consumption records, census data, climate normalization, and tourism registers. Applied to Alicante, Spain, between 2022 and 2024, the model uses a thermal-correction algorithm to isolate temperature-driven water demand and K-means clustering with Dynamic Time Warping to classify neighborhood seasonal patterns. Out-of-sample validation for 2024 achieved a Mean Absolute Percentage Error of 6.34% and an R-squared of 0.9874, capturing a summer population surge of 8.78% (+32,749 people) citywide, with coastal tourist zones growing by over 50% and wealthier central districts shrinking by up to 22.2%.
en.why: It provides a low-cost, privacy-preserving method to measure highly dynamic, seasonal population shifts at a neighborhood scale without relying on restrictive mobile phone data or static census records.
